## Teaching points

1. Previous crystal confirmation and a typical attack favor gout. Evaluate for joint infection when the course or examination is atypical.
2. Prior crystal confirmation supports gout but does not exclude a concurrent infection when new features suggest one.
3. Choose anti-inflammatory treatment around comorbidities and preferences; a single named NSAID is not the only valid option.
4. Recurrent attacks warrant follow-up to discuss long-term urate lowering. Do not present dietary blame as the whole management plan.
